claim: RAUC marks the target slot non-bootable before writing it and marks it bootable (active/primary) only after all slots are written.
RAUC's GRUB backend implements mark-good as <slot>_OK=1,<slot>_TRY=0 and mark-bad as <slot>_OK=0,<slot>_TRY=0 in grubenv.
RAUC's GRUB backend activates a slot by setting <slot>_OK=1, <slot>_TRY=0 and putting it first in ORDER.
RAUC's reference GRUB script boots the first slot in ORDER with OK=1 and TRY=0, then sets its TRY=1 before booting, so an uncommitted slot gets exactly one boot attempt.
RAUC docs say the grubenv must live outside the redundant rootfs partitions, e.g. /EFI/BOOT/grubenv on the EFI partition, with load_env/save_env --file in grub.cfg.
RAUC docs recommend a systemd service that runs `rauc status mark-good` after the relevant services have come up.

Home Assistant OS's x86 GRUB script stores grubenv on the ESP and allows up to 3 boot attempts per slot (TRY<3) before falling back.
The Home Assistant Supervisor commits the booted slot by calling RAUC Mark(GOOD, 'booted') over D-Bus in its mark_healthy job, i.e. HAOS's gate is 'Supervisor is running', not 'all apps healthy'.

CRA (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847) applies from 2027-12-11; Article 14 (reporting) applies from 2026-09-11; Chapter IV (notified bodies) from 2026-06-11 (Art. 71(2)).

CRA Art. 13(8): support period must reflect expected use time and be at least five years (shorter only if expected use is shorter); factors include the support periods of integrated third-party components providing core functions and the availability of the operating environment.
CRA Art. 13(9): each security update made available during the support period must remain available for at least 10 years after issue or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer.

CRA Art. 13(10): for subsequent substantially modified versions of a software product, the manufacturer may meet Annex I Part II(2) only for the latest version, provided users of earlier versions get the latest version free of charge and without extra cost to adjust their hardware/software environment.
CRA Art. 13(19): the end date of the support period (at least month and year) must be clearly specified at the time of purchase; where feasible users are notified when support ends.
CRA Art. 13(23): a manufacturer that ceases operations must inform market surveillance authorities and, as far as possible, users before cessation takes effect.

CRA Art. 14(1)-(2),(8): actively exploited vulnerabilities must be notified via the ENISA single reporting platform: early warning within 24 h, vulnerability notification within 72 h, final report within 14 days after a fix is available; impacted users must be informed.

CRA Annex I Part I(2)(c): products must ensure vulnerabilities can be addressed through security updates, including, where applicable, automatic security updates enabled as a default setting with a clear and easy opt-out, notification of updates, and the option to temporarily postpone them.

CRA Annex I Part I(2): secure-by-default configuration including reset to original state (b); confidentiality incl. encryption at rest/in transit (e); integrity (f); attack-surface limitation (j); logging with opt-out (l); secure permanent removal of all data and settings (m).

CRA Annex I Part II: SBOM in a commonly used machine-readable format covering at least top-level dependencies (1); security updates separate from functionality updates where technically feasible (2); coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy (5); security updates free of charge with advisories (8).

CRA Annex III lists 'Operating systems' (Class I, item 11), 'Boot managers' (I-8), VPN products (I-5), routers (I-12), identity management systems (I-1) and smart home general purpose virtual assistants (I-16); Class II includes 'Hypervisors and container runtime systems'.

CRA Art. 32(2): a Class I important product whose manufacturer has not applied (or only partly applied) harmonised standards, common specifications or an EU certification scheme must use EU-type examination (module B+C) or full quality assurance (module H), i.e. a notified body.

CRA Art. 32(5): manufacturers of products qualifying as free and open-source software in Annex III categories may use any Art. 32(1) procedure, including internal control (module A), provided the technical documentation is made public when the product is placed on the market.

CRA Art. 3: 'manufacturer' covers products marketed under its name whether for payment, monetisation or free of charge; an 'open-source software steward' is a legal person other than a manufacturer; recital 15 says intention to monetise, e.g. via a platform through which other services are monetised, indicates commercial activity.
CRA Art. 21-22: an importer or distributor placing a product under its own name/trademark, or anyone carrying out a substantial modification and making it available, is treated as a manufacturer.
CRA Art. 69(2)-(3): products placed on the market before 2027-12-11 are subject only if substantially modified afterwards, but Art. 14 reporting applies to all in-scope products regardless.

systemd-cryptenroll: --tpm2-public-key binds to a signed PCR policy (default PCR 11, any UKI with a valid PCR signature) so measurements can change on every update while signatures stay valid; literal --tpm2-pcrs binding breaks after updates; PCRs 7, 11 and 14 (with shim/MOK) are the general recommendation; --tpm2-pcrlock since systemd 255.

Raspberry Pi secure boot: boot ROM verifies against a hash of the customer RSA-2048 public key in OTP; on BCM2712 the customer key also signs the EEPROM bootloader; the bootloader verifies boot.img with boot.sig; an OTP device-unique secret unlocks a LUKS root (AES-XTS on BCM2712).

Raspberry Pi bootloader: if secure-boot is enabled, tryboot loads tryboot.img instead of boot.img, and tryboot_a_b is implicitly set when loading files from within a boot.img ramdisk (partition-level A/B).

Raspberry Pi docs: 'Raspberry Pi computers do not have a hardware protected key store'; rpi-sb-provisioner: generating the BCM2712 device key 'writes to OTP permanently and cannot be undone'; JTAG lock and signing-key programming are irreversible.

Jetson Orin secure boot (r36.4.4): the OEM generates PKC/SBK keys; fuse burning is irreversible; three PKC keys can be fused and the first two revoked; RSA-3K and ECDSA P-256/P-521 (RSA-2048 unsupported on Orin); UEFI Secure Boot enabled at flash cannot be disabled without reflashing; A/B kernel images must be signed with the db key.

Jetson Orin disk encryption (r36.4.4): LUKS AES-XTS-256; the OP-TEE luks-srv TA derives a per-device passphrase from the EKB disk-encryption key, ECID and disk UUID; mass-flashed generic keys are replaced per device at first boot.

Jetson Orin firmware TPM (r36.4.4): TPM 2.0 reference implementation as an OP-TEE TA with measured boot into PCRs; needs fused KDK0 and offline EK-certificate provisioning; online provisioning not yet available.

Debian trixie kernel config enables batman-adv (CONFIG_BATMAN_ADV=m), 802.11s mesh (CONFIG_MAC80211_MESH=y), WireGuard (m), PTP clock (y) and the TSN qdiscs taprio and etf (m).
Debian trixie packages libopen62541-1.4 (OPC UA, version 1.4.11.1-1) for amd64, arm64, armhf, riscv64 and others.
Debian trixie packages mosquitto 2.0.21, libmodbus 3.1.11, can-utils 2023.03, batctl 2025.0, linuxptp 4.2 and nats-server 2.10.27.
Debian trixie builds wpa_supplicant and hostapd with Wi-Fi Easy Connect (CONFIG_DPP=y, CONFIG_DPP2=y); wpa_supplicant also has CONFIG_MESH=y.
NATS server implements MQTT v3.1.1 with QoS 0, 1 and 2; a client requesting MQTT v5 is rejected at connect with CONNACK return code 1 (unacceptable protocol version).
NATS server added 'MQTT SparkplugB Aware support' on 2024-04-03 (PR #5241); server/mqtt.go implements Sparkplug Aware rules (NBIRTH/DBIRTH stored and retained under $sparkplug/certificates/...).
NATS converts MQTT topics to subjects by replacing '/' with '.' and '.' with '//', so Sparkplug 'spBv1.0/...' topics become subjects containing '//'.
Sparkplug: 'Any fully MQTT v3.1.1 or v5.0 MQTT Server will meet the requirements'; a compliant server MUST support QoS 0, QoS 1, Will Messages (with retain and QoS 1) and the retain flag.
Eclipse Mosquitto implements MQTT 5.0, 3.1.1 and 3.1 and is dual licensed EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause.
NanoMQ supports MQTT 3.1.1/3.1 and 5.0 (enhanced auth and server redirection unsupported), is MIT licensed; latest release 0.25.7 on 2026-10-21.

EMQX 5.9.0 and later is under Business Source License 1.1; the Additional Use Grant excludes offering it to third parties on a hosted or embedded basis (integrating into a product offered to third parties); change license Apache-2.0 after four years.
Reticulum is under the custom 'Reticulum License', which forbids use in any system able to purposefully harm humans and any use in creating AI/ML training datasets.

The Meshtastic ATAK plugin (GPL-3.0) sends CoT through the Meshtastic Android app, needs ATAK-CIV, defaults to hop limit 3, caps file transfer at 56 KB (Short_Turbo preset) and can relay between the mesh and TAK servers.

Meshtastic MQTT gateways publish on msh/REGION/2/e/CHANNEL/USERID (protobuf) and .../json/... ; JSON is not supported on nRF52; the docs advise against the default key on a private broker. Firmware is GPL-3.0.
TAK Server source published by the TAK Product Center on GitHub is GPL-3.0; the latest public tag is 5.7-RELEASE-14 (2026-04-03).

TAK Server 5.7 Configuration Guide: supported OS include Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) and Ubuntu 22; server needs 4 cores, 8 GB RAM, 40 GB disk; a Pi 4 8 GB is recommended for a minimal setup; Java 17 required; single server recommended under 500 users; Docker and hardened Docker bundles exist.
Debian 13 trixie has no openjdk-17 source package (it ships openjdk-21), so TAK Server's Java 17 host install is not native on Debian 13.
ATAK-CIV source is GPL-3.0 in TAK-Product-Center/atak-civ; the older deptofdefense/AndroidTacticalAssaultKit-CIV repo is archived.

OpenTAKServer is GPL-3.0 (release 1.8.1, 2026-11-06), has installer scripts for Ubuntu and Raspberry Pi, supports ATAK 4.8+, iTAK and WinTAK, needs Python 3.10+ and RabbitMQ, and its docs link a 'TAK Meshtastic Gateway' page.
FreeTAKServer (EPL-2.0) has had no push to its main repo since 2024-10-29.
CloudTAK is AGPL-3.0; its README says Docker Compose exposes the core map but a full AWS deployment is still required for the full ETL features.
Home Assistant: HA OS is the recommended installation type; HA Container installations have no access to apps; HA OS on Raspberry Pi needs a Pi 4 or 5 with at least 2 GB RAM.
Home Assistant's Matter integration: running the Matter app on HA OS is 'the only supported option'; a standalone Docker Matter Server is unsupported; Matter needs local IPv6 multicast and mDNS.
umbrelOS runs its Home Assistant app with network_mode host, privileged: true, and the host /dev and /run/dbus mounted into the container.

Olares runs Home Assistant (2026.10.0) as a k8s Deployment (requests 500m CPU / 1 GiB, limits 2 CPU / 3 GiB) that becomes privileged only when the USB_PASSTHROUGH option is on; its manifest warns this is about host root and says network coordinators via socket:// need no passthrough.

By directory name, the Umbrel catalog (406 entries at the pinned SHA) includes mosquitto, zigbee2mqtt, node-red, esphome and influxdb; the Olares catalog (408 entries) has only homeassistant, frigate and grafana in this area; neither has a TAK, Meshtastic, OPC UA or LoRaWAN app.
ESPHome's native API reboots the node when no authenticated client connects within reboot_timeout, which defaults to 15 min (0s disables); the API supports a 32-byte base64 encryption key.
ESPHome switch restore_mode defaults to ALWAYS_OFF (the switch initialises OFF at boot) unless the platform sets another default.
ESPHome's license: the C/C++ runtime is GPLv3, the Python codebase and other parts are MIT.
ChirpStack (MIT, v4.20.0) MQTT integration publishes uplinks on application/APPLICATION_ID/device/DEV_EUI/event/up and takes downlinks on .../command/down, JSON-encoded.

Moxa Industrial Linux 4 is based on Debian 13 (MIL3 on Debian 11); MIL4 support runs to Aug 2035 and MIL3 to Dec 2031; Moxa lists an IEC 62443-4-2 Security Level 2 certification declaration for UC-1200A/2200A/3400A/4400A/8600A with MIL4 (v1.0, 2026-07-02) and for UC-8200 with MIL3 (2022-11-28).

Linux Foundation press release (2026-09-28): the Civil Infrastructure Platform achieved IEC 62443-4-1 and 4-2 compliance; adopters keep responsibility for their own products; CIP estimates up to 70% less compliance effort.
IEC 62443-4-2:2019 (edition 1.0, published 2019-02-27, stability date 2027) gives technical security requirements and capability levels (SL-C) for IACS components.
NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 (Guide to OT Security) is final since 2023-09-28; a Rev. 4 initial public draft has comments due 2026-11-30.

Siemens Industrial Edge Own Device (IEOD) is an image 'based on the Linux Debian 12 (bookworm) distribution' and Industrial Edge Device Kit 1.24.1 for x86-64 UEFI hardware (min 1 core, 2 GB RAM); it does not support Arm; it encrypts disks only when TPM 2.0 is present.
Siemens' open SIMATIC IOT2050 image (meta-iot2050, MIT) is built with Isar as distro 'iot2050-debian' and pulls isar-cip-core.
Revolution Pi's current image is 'RevPi Trixie', based on Raspberry Pi OS (Debian), with a linux-image-6.18.*-revpi0-rpi-v8 kernel; RevPi Connect 5 is supported.
The Raspberry Pi kernel tree (rpi-6.18.y and rpi-6.12.y) has a bcm2711_rt_defconfig (Pi 4) but no real-time defconfig for bcm2712 (Pi 5).
Raspberry Pi's security architecture stores a device-unique secret in OTP 'protected by software mechanisms' and uses the VideoCore to sign with it; the page mentions no TPM.

FIDO Alliance lists FDO 1.1 and 2.0 as Proposed Standards dated 2026-04-02, 'Securing FDO Credentials in the TPM' as a Review Draft (2023-10-10) and the Voucher Transfer Protocol 1.0 as a Review Draft (2026-10-01).

IEEE 802.1AR-2018 (Secure Device Identity) is active: a supplier-provided Initial Device Identifier (IDevID) is cryptographically bound to the device and can be supplemented by Local DevIDs.
Rugix Ctrl documents ready-made fleet-management integrations with Nexigon, thin-edge.io, Memfault and Mender, and keeps the update engine independent of any fleet backend.
thin-edge.io (Apache-2.0, release 2.1.0 on 2026-11-04) is a cloud-agnostic IoT framework that officially supports Rugix Bakery and Rugix Ctrl.
Flight Control (Apache-2.0) 'works best on image-based Linux operating systems running bootc or ostree' and does OS updates via bootc or rpm-ostree with Greenboot rollback.
k3s server sizing: 2 CPU/4 GB for 0-350 agents, 4/8 GB for 351-900, 8/16 GB for 901-1800, 16+/32 GB for 1800+; minimum server 2 cores/2 GB, agent 1 core/512 MB.
